summary:
- MARSWALK is a web application that simulates Mars exploration mission planning, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project transforms terrain data, imagery, and rover traverses into an interactive interface that allows users to explore Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Meridiani Planum. The application provides a real map, scientific waypoints, location illustrations, MOLA elevation data, and rover tracks from Perseverance and Curiosity.

- Because Mars does not have GPS for human explorers, MARSWALK simulates a manual navigation process. Users can start a mission, track travel time between locations, complete research activities, and monitor oxygen consumption within an eight-hour EVA limit. Activities include photography, geological analysis, mineral research, and sample collection.

- The project helps students and the public understand how a Mars mission is planned while connecting scientific data with an accessible interactive experience.
details:
- MARSWALK is an interactive web application that simulates a Mars exploration mission control center. Users can select a region, view the real map, inspect scientific waypoints, and build a survey plan within the eight-hour limit of an EVA.

- The application focuses on three main regions:
+ Jezero Crater: Octavia E. Butler Landing, Three Forks Sample Depot, Delta Front, Upper Fan, Margin Unit, and Neretva Vallis.
+ Gale Crater: Bradbury Landing, Cumberland, and Yellowknife Bay.
+ Meridiani Planum: Eagle Crater, Vista Alcove, Fram Crater, and Eagle Base/Airlock.

- Each location includes information about its geological context, scientific objectives, minerals, elevation, slope, atmosphere, radiation, terrain hazards, sample collection tasks, and reference imagery. User-provided images are attached to the map according to their corresponding regions to support terrain identification. Locations without verified NASA coordinates are displayed as approximate positions with clear source notes.

- Since humans cannot use GPS on Mars, MARSWALK includes a manual mission mode. When the user presses the start button, the system explains that live GPS positioning is unavailable and offers manual navigation. Users can then:
+ Follow a mission countdown timer.
+ Travel through the waypoints in sequence.
+ View the estimated travel time between locations.
+ Complete research activities at each location.
+ Replace the planned travel time with the actual time spent.
+ Monitor oxygen usage within the eight-hour limit.
+ Pause, resume, or end the mission.
+ Record mission progress and collected scientific data.

- The real map uses Leaflet to display the basemap, markers, information popups, map layers, and rover routes. Terrain data is referenced from MOLA. Surface and orbital imagery are connected to NASA Mars Trek, CTX, HiRISE, and rover mission data. The Jezero and Gale routes are based on recorded rover traverse segments. Meridiani uses the verified Eagle Crater coordinates, while the other reference positions are estimated from the user-provided EVA diagram.

- The interface is built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. It also uses Leaflet, model-viewer, and separate JavaScript modules for maps, location data, mission timing, language translation, and HUD simulation. The system supports Vietnamese, English, Russian, and Japanese. When users change the language, the entire interface updates immediately without reloading the page, including notifications, location names, buttons, mission tables, safety information, and map content.

- The project provides a visual way to learn planetary science. Instead of only reading geological data or viewing isolated images, users experience the mission-planning process directly: selecting a location, evaluating terrain, allocating time, managing oxygen, carrying out research, and returning to base. This makes concepts such as terrain, minerals, rover routes, samples, and EVA hazards easier to understand.

- MARSWALK is intended to support STEM education, encourage interest in planetary science, and demonstrate how NASA data can be transformed into an interactive learning tool. The project can be expanded to support additional missions, higher-resolution DEM data, more rover datasets, classroom activities, and custom exploration scenarios.

- The team considered scientific accuracy, the distinction between verified and simulated data, image provenance, the limitations of GPS on Mars, usability on computers and mobile devices, multilingual support, accessibility for new users, and transparent presentation of incomplete or approximate data.
